title: Archaeologists Discover Denisovan Remains in China and Reveal How They Lived
text:
Hidden among thousands of animal bones, several fragile fragments are reshaping what scientists know about one of humanity’s most mysterious relatives.

In Bianfu Cave in southwestern China, archaeologists have discovered new Denisovan fossils – remains of a mysterious group of ancient humans. The finds offer new insights into how they lived, what they ate, and the environmental conditions to which they adapted.

As reported by CNN

The material includes four teeth, a fragment of an arm bone, and two pieces of a skull. They bring the total number of known Denisovan remains to more than 20. The cave, located in the mountains of Yunnan Province, has become an important site for studying human evolution.

Alongside seven Denisovan remains, scientists found stone and bone tools, ancient plant pollen, and animal bones. The results of two studies published in the journal Nature indicate that humans lived in the area among coniferous forests approximately 167,000–134,000 years ago.

At first, we found individual teeth, and later we discovered bones among a huge number of animal remains. In the beginning, these fragments were extremely difficult to spot.

– Hao Li

Hao Li noted that Bianfu is the first site in southern China where Denisovan remains have been directly associated with a large quantity of cultural material. This makes it possible to determine the age of the finds more precisely and reconstruct certain aspects of ancient people’s daily lives.

Until now, knowledge about the Denisovans had been based largely on isolated and incomplete finds. The group was identified in 2010 through ancient DNA from a small finger bone discovered in Denisova Cave in Siberia. It was the first time an unknown group of ancient humans had been identified solely through genetic evidence.

Denisovans are believed to have lived in various parts of Asia. Today, the highest levels of Denisovan DNA are found among populations in Southeast Asia and Oceania. This indicates that Denisovans interbred with modern humans tens of thousands of years ago.

Bianfu is only the third site where the presence of Denisovans has been directly confirmed. It shows that members of this group may have adapted to highly diverse environments – from the mountainous regions of Siberia and the highlands of Tibet to the subtropical climate of Yunnan.

During the excavations, archaeologists examined around 60,000 bone fragments. Approximately 20 of them may have belonged to hominins. Although no ancient DNA survived in the remains, amino acid variants characteristic of Denisovan proteins were found in three bones and two teeth. Two additional teeth were assigned to the group based on their shape and comparison with known specimens.

Yunnan’s warmer climate probably accelerated the degradation of DNA. Proteins proved more resilient, preserving molecular signatures that made it possible to determine the remains’ identity.

Researchers opened three excavation pits in the cave, reaching depths of up to 6.6 meters. Human remains were found in only one of them, in two layers dated to 167,000–134,000 years ago. Stone tools appeared in ten layers, indicating that the cave was used from approximately 190,000 to 70,000 years ago.

The finds indicate that the Denisovans:

made tools from stone and bone;

hunted water buffalo, gaur, red deer, and sika deer;

extracted bone marrow as a source of food;

used a simple but flexible stone-working technology.

Hao Li described this technology as practical. According to him, the cave’s inhabitants did not spend much time making stone tools but consistently used the same approach to produce them.

Scientists suggest that Denisovans may have occupied the cave throughout much of this period. To test this possibility, they plan to examine the soil for hominin DNA.

Among the new material is the first known Denisovan arm bone. The fragment shows that the radius was short and somewhat resembled the corresponding bone in Neanderthals. Paleoanthropologist Ryan McRae suggested that the attachment site of the biceps muscle may have enabled more efficient bending of the elbow.

The site itself is the most interesting thing. It shows how Denisovans used the same place over a long period of time and fills geographical gaps in our understanding of this group.

– Ryan McRae

In 2025, researchers led by Qiaomei Fu linked a skull known as Dragon Man to the Denisovans. It was found in Harbin after spending decades at the bottom of a well. Genetic analysis connected the specimen with the Denisovans, for whom the scientific name Homo longi was proposed.

Despite these new discoveries, the Denisovans’ appearance, way of life, and reasons for extinction remain poorly understood. The material from Yunnan may help fill these gaps, as the region had a mild climate, abundant plant and animal resources, and was likely a natural crossroads between northern and southern Asia.
